drivingQuestion: What does the mishna's clause 'he is like one of the brothers' teach, since it seems obvious?
outcomeNote: the clause teaches he is not penalized and inherits equally

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ פְּשִׁיטָא! סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא חֲלִיצָה בִּמְקוֹם יִבּוּם קָיְימָא, וְנִשְׁקוֹל כּוּלְּהוּ נִכְסֵי, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The Gemara asks with regard to the opening clause of the mishna: The fact that one who performs ḥalitza does not gain any special rights to the inheritance of the deceased brother «is obvious;» why did the mishna teach it? The Gemara answers: «It could enter your mind to say» that the «ḥalitza takes the place of the levirate marriage and» therefore the brother who performs ḥalitza «should take all the property» in the same way as one who consummates the levirate marriage. Therefore, the mishna «teaches us» that this is not the case.

segments.he: אִי הָכִי, הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאֶחָד מִן הָאַחִים — אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּאֶחָד מִן הָאַחִים מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ!
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «If so,» that the mishna’s point is to teach that by performing ḥalitza one is not afforded any additional rights to the inheritance, why is the mishna formulated as: «He is like» any «one of the» other «brothers,» placing the emphasis on what he gains? «It should have» instead taught: «He is» still «only like one of the» other «brothers,» which would emphasize the mishna’s point that by performing ḥalitza he does not gain any additional rights.

segments.he: אֶלָּא, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: הוֹאִיל וְאַפְסְדַהּ מִיִּבּוּם, לִקְנְסֵיהּ, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.
segments.en: «Rather,» the mishna needs to teach the opening clause in this manner because «it could enter your mind to say» that «since» by performing ḥalitza with his yevama «he caused her to forfeit» the possibility of consummating the «levirate marriage, he should be penalized» and should forfeit any entitlement to his brother’s property. Therefore the mishna «teaches us» that this is not so.
